[{"order":1,"type":"heading","text":"Debugging tf.function and NaN Issues in TensorFlow"},{"order":2,"type":"paragraph","text":"TensorFlow relies heavily on tf.function to compile and optimize Python code into high-performance graph execution. While this boosts performance, it obscures standard Python debugging techniques. Furthermore, encountering Not a Number (NaN) values during training can derail model convergence. This tutorial covers advanced strategies to debug compiled graph functions and trace the root causes of NaN instabilities."},{"order":3,"type":"subheading","text":"1. Fallback to Eager Execution"},{"order":4,"type":"paragraph","text":"When a tf.function fails, the stack trace often points inside the TensorFlow C++ runtime rather than your Python lines. The quickest way to debug is to temporarily disable graph compilation."},{"order":5,"type":"code","text":"tf.config.run_functions_eagerly(True)"},{"order":6,"type":"paragraph","text":"Running eagerly forces TensorFlow to execute operations line-by-line, allowing standard tools like pdb or print statements to function normally. Remember to disable eager execution once debugging is complete to restore performance."},{"order":7,"type":"subheading","text":"2. Using tf.print for Graph Inspection"},{"order":8,"type":"paragraph","text":"Standard Python print statements only evaluate during the tracing phase of a tf.function, not during actual execution. To output tensor values inside a compiled graph, use tf.print."},{"order":9,"type":"code","text":"@tf.function
def train_step(x, y):
    predictions = model(x)
    loss = loss_fn(y, predictions)
    tf.print("Current Loss: ", loss)
    return loss"},{"order":10,"type":"subheading","text":"3. Detecting NaNs Early with tf.debugging"},{"order":11,"type":"paragraph","text":"NaN values often propagate silently through layers before causing a catastrophic model failure. TensorFlow provides specific assertion ops to catch NaNs the moment they appear."},{"order":12,"type":"code","text":"@tf.function
def robust_step(x, y):
    tf.debugging.assert_all_finite(x, "Input tensor contains NaN or Inf")
    grads = compute_gradients(x, y)
    tf.debugging.assert_all_finite(grads, "Gradients exploded to NaN!")
    return grads"},{"order":13,"type":"subheading","text":"4. Common Causes of NaN and How to Fix Them"},{"order":14,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Division by zero: Add a small epsilon value (e.g., 1e-7) to denominators inside operations like log or division."},{"order":15,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Logarithms of zero: Ensure inputs to tf.math.log are strictly positive."},{"order":16,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Gradient explosion: Use tf.clip_by_norm or tf.clip_by_value to constrain gradient updates."},{"order":17,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Mixed precision: When using float16, scale your loss using tf.keras.mixed_precision.LossScaleOptimizer to prevent underflow."},{"order":18,"type":"subheading","text":"Conclusion"},{"order":19,"type":"paragraph","text":"Debugging compiled TensorFlow graphs requires a systematic shift from traditional Python debugging. By leveraging eager execution switches, tf.print, and robust assertions from tf.debugging, you can isolate and resolve graph errors and NaN propagations efficiently."}]
